insights.insight: Across 23 November to 3 December 2024, Oromia recorded 33 political-violence events and 146 fatalities, with zero demonstrations, indicating contention was expressed through clashes, attacks, and remote violence rather than protests.
insights.context: Intro and event/fatality overview citing ACLED counts and types [1][2][3][4].

insights.insight: Demobilization events—agreements and surrenders—occurred with zero fatalities and were concentrated in North Shewa, West Shewa, and Guji, highlighting a narrow geographic and temporal window of non-lethal ‘peace optics.’
insights.context: Split-screen framing and mapping of ‘Strategic developments’ with zero fatalities, clustered around 2–3 December [2][5][6][7][10][11].

insights.insight: Violence peaked around 25–26 November with roughly 10 fatalities per day from battles, and on 28 November with 11 deaths from explosions/remote violence and 10 from violence against civilians, showing compressed lethal spikes.
insights.context: Daily distribution and lethality patterns, highlighting 28 November as deadliest date [5][4].

insights.insight: Civilians accounted for 31 of the 146 fatalities, while most deaths stemmed from battles between OLF‑OLA and federal forces and from strikes/shelling, indicating combat and remote attacks drove lethality.
insights.context: Fatality composition by event type and actors [2].

insights.insight: North Shewa experienced a one‑day burst of three agreement-type events on 2 December, centered on Jiru Dada (Dera woreda), making it the top site by event count in the window and emblematic of the demobilization push.
insights.context: Location prominence and specific agreements in Jiru Dada/Dera [12][7][3][13][14].

insights.insight: Approximately 800 OLF‑OLA fighters from Central Oromia reportedly entered rehabilitation in Ambo (West Shewa) on 3 December following a 1 December peace deal, reinforcing the Central Oromia demobilization narrative.
insights.context: West Shewa demobilization sequence around Ambo [3][10].

insights.insight: Even near demobilization hubs, violence persisted: VAC incidents in Enewari and Muke Turi (North Shewa) and Minare (West Shewa) occurred within days of agreements, each causing at least one death.
insights.context: Temporal proximity analysis linking agreements to nearby VAC events with single fatalities [16][17].

insights.insight: Central Oromia’s demobilization was spatially tight and temporally brief—primarily 2–3 December—and did not extend across the region, resembling a negotiated corridor rather than a broad de-escalation.
insights.context: Clustering of agreement events and limited geographic spread [12][7][3][6].

insights.insight: Peripheral zones bore the brunt of civilian harm: East Wellega recorded the most VAC incidents (four, five deaths total), while Arsi had fewer VAC events but higher lethality (two incidents causing 13 civilian deaths).
insights.context: Zone-level VAC distribution and lethality contrast between East Wellega and Arsi [22][10][11].

insights.insight: Single high-fatality VAC incidents shaped risk profiles in South West Shewa (six killed in Tulu Bolo) and Horo Gudru Wellega (about five killed in Jawij Migir), underscoring episodic but deadly threats.
insights.context: Examples of concentrated lethal events defining local risk [15][22][23].

insights.insight: No VAC incidents were recorded in demobilizing North and West Shewa during the window, while Guji saw both an agreement and a non-fatal VAC incident, indicating uneven de-escalation across zones.
insights.context: Spatial mapping of VAC presence/absence and agreements [24][10][25][11].

insights.insight: OLF‑OLA perpetrated the deadliest civilian attacks in Arsi, killing nine in Sole Ferekasa and four in Gobesa, yielding high median lethality per VAC incident for this actor in the period.
insights.context: Actor-location breakdown of VAC incidents and fatalities attributed to OLF‑OLA [24][23][26].

insights.insight: A Fano Youth Militia ambush on Oromo traders in Jawij Migir (Horo Gudru Wellega) left about five dead, making Fano’s single recorded attack among the period’s most lethal VAC events.
insights.context: Specific lethal event attributed to Fano Youth Militia [21][24][23][26].

insights.insight: Unidentified armed groups contributed to civilian harm variability: six killed in Tulu Bolo (South West Shewa) versus zero fatalities in Ayana (East Wellega), reflecting volatility within this category.
insights.context: Contrasting outcomes for unidentified gunmen across locations [24][23][26].

insights.insight: Ethiopian military personnel appeared in five VAC incidents across West/East Wellega and Guji, causing seven civilian deaths total—more frequent but less lethal on average than OLF‑OLA’s attacks.
insights.context: State force implication and relative lethality in VAC incidents [24][22][26][8].

insights.insight: East Wellega simultaneously functioned as a battlefront and a site of repeat lower-scale civilian targeting, with battles there producing 13 fatalities during the window.
insights.context: Battle fatalities and dual-threat profile for East Wellega [21][15][8][9].

insights.insight: For civilians along the Wellega–Arsi corridor, risk was defined by whether a small number of highly lethal incidents struck specific routes or markets on a given day, rather than by sustained large offensives.
